overview.text: Panic disorder is characterised by recurrent unexpected panic attacks that are not restricted to a particular situation, together with persistent concern or behaviour change for at least a month afterwards. ICD-11 now separates panic disorder from agoraphobia as two distinct diagnoses that can be assigned together, rather than the two being alternatives.

The defining psychological mechanism is not excessive fear but a misreading of bodily sensation, so treatment targets the catastrophic interpretation and the avoidance that follows, and an SSRI that worked before is preferred over switching drug class.

Panic disorder is modestly heritable. Polygenic scores discriminate affected people from controls only weakly, with the best area under the curve around 0.60 in the largest study, so genetics has no diagnostic role at present.

description.text: Abrupt surges of intense fear with palpitations, sweating, tremor, breathlessness, choking sensation, chest pain, nausea and derealisation, peaking within minutes. The attack is experienced as arriving from out of the blue, which is what distinguishes the disorder from fear in a specific situation.

The sense of imminent death, losing control or going mad, and the resulting conviction that the sensation means something grave. This appraisal, not the bodily sensation itself, is the treatment target and the reason CBT outperforms reassurance.
Persistent fear of the next attack, which itself raises baseline arousal and makes the next attack more likely. It is what converts attacks from isolated events into a chronic disorder.

Withdrawal from situations where an attack would be embarrassing or unwitnessed, such as public transport, crowds or being alone, along with reassurance-seeking and escaping early. Maintaining this avoidance is the main obstacle to recovery.

Repeated presentation with physical complaints and requests for investigations, and conversely, over-reliance on home monitoring devices. Unnecessary medical investigation is a recognised harm of this presentation.

Depressive disorder frequently co-occurs, and alcohol or sedative self-medication is common and then becomes its own problem. Guidelines advise treating both rather than treating the panic attacks alone.

atlasLabels: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci)
Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle anterior part)

claim.text: The interoceptive network formed by the insula, anterior cingulate and amygdala represents internal bodily state, and in panic disorder the signal from that network is amplified and misread as danger. The fear-circuit model confirmed in social anxiety disorder is applied here as a shared model rather than as a measured finding in this disorder.

Brainstem nuclei generate the cardiorespiratory and ventilatory components of a panic attack, and hyperventilation lowers carbon dioxide which further amplifies the sensation of threat. These structures are resolved in the atlas, unlike the deeper nuclei that are not.

function.text: A normal bodily change such as a heart rate increase is amplified in the insula, assigned a threatening meaning in the anterior cingulate and orbitofrontal cortex, and confirmed by the amygdala. Breaking the appraisal rather than the sensation is why cognitive behavioural therapy is first line.

Avoidance is learned: contexts paired with an attack acquire negative value, and the dopamine-modulated striatal loop that encodes this cost is why the patient progressively narrows their world. Re-approaching those contexts is what reverses it.

The two brainstem systems that every first-line drug acts on are not resolved by this atlas and appear as calibrated markers. Hyperventilation and the resulting fall in carbon dioxide add to the adrenergic surge, which is why breathing and pacing skills form part of treatment.

neurochemistry.alteration: Reduced serotonergic modulation of the interoceptive signal

claim.text: SSRIs are first line and the preferred choice is a drug that previously helped the individual, with 5-HT1A partial agonism available where dependence is the concern.

neurochemistry.alteration: Adrenergic surge amplifying cardiac and tremor symptoms

claim.text: The adrenergic surge during an attack is what supplies the palpitations and tremor that the patient then misreads, which is the loop that cognitive work and noradrenergic drugs both target.
Panic attacks can be provoked by raising carbon dioxide, and hyperventilation during an attack lowers it and amplifies the sensation, so ventilation is both a symptom and a maintaining mechanism.

neurochemistry.alteration: Excitatory transmission within the appraisal loop

atlasLabels: Insula (Subcentral gyrus and ant. and post. sulci)

claim.text: Excitatory transmission between insula, cingulate and orbitofrontal cortex carries the misread signal, and calcium-channel ligands that reduce excitatory release are an option when first-line drugs are unsuitable.

architecture.text: Panic disorder is modestly heritable and polygenic. In the largest study of polygenic discrimination, combining scores improved classification but the best area under the curve was only about 0.60, which the authors themselves describe as modest.

The gene listed here encodes the pharmacological target of first-line treatment rather than a susceptibility gene, because no susceptibility gene has been established for this disorder. No genetic test has clinical use.

finding.text: Polygenic scores distinguish affected people from controls with an area under the curve of roughly 0.60 at best, which is far too weak for diagnosis. This is an honest ceiling on current genetic prediction for this disorder.

The insula, anterior cingulate and amygdala form the interoceptive circuit whose amplification is the accepted model, confirmed as a shared fear-circuit model in social anxiety disorder rather than measured directly in this disorder.
Raised carbon dioxide provokes attacks in susceptible people and is studied as an experimental challenge, but it has no role as a routine clinical test.

pathway.step: First line: SSRI and cognitive behavioural therapy

claim.text: Guidelines recommend an SSRI or SNRI and cognitive behavioural therapy as first line, and a previous good response to a particular drug is the strongest guide to which to use. Full-dose treatment may be needed earlier than for depression because the target is avoidance.
A 5-HT1A partial agonist is preferred where there is a history of substance misuse or benzodiazepine dependence, because it gives anxiolysis without a withdrawal syndrome.
Benzodiazepines abort attacks quickly but are limited to short-term crisis use because tolerance and dependence develop within weeks, and they do not treat the avoidance that maintains the disorder.

Depression and alcohol or sedative self-medication are treated actively, and unnecessary medical investigation arising from health anxiety is itself a harm to be avoided by explaining the mechanism clearly.

Recovery requires re-approaching avoided situations, since the avoidance is what sustains the disorder. A graded return to public transport, crowds and being alone is the practical goal of therapy rather than symptom reduction alone.

tour.title: 1 · Attacks that arrive from nowhere
tour.text: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks not tied to a particular situation, with a month or more of persistent worry or behaviour change afterwards.

tour.title: 2 · The body is misread, not feared
tour.text: The insula amplifies a normal bodily change, the anterior cingulate and orbitofrontal cortex give it a threatening meaning, and the amygdala confirms it. The appraisal is the treatment target.

tour.title: 3 · The brainstem generators
tour.text: Cardiorespiratory and ventilatory components come from brainstem structures that this atlas does resolve, unlike the deeper nuclei it does not.

tour.title: 4 · Avoidance is the illness
tour.text: Contexts paired with an attack acquire negative value in a striatal loop, and the world narrows. Re-approaching them is what reverses the disorder.

tour.title: 5 · The two drug systems
tour.text: Raphe and locus coeruleus drive the interoceptive and adrenergic signals, and both appear as schematic markers because the atlas does not resolve them.

tour.title: 6 · Genetics has a low ceiling
tour.text: The best polygenic discrimination reaches an area under the curve near 0.60, which the source calls modest, so there is no genetic test here.

quiz.question: What ICD-11 code covers panic disorder?
quiz.explanation: ICD-11 code 6B01 is panic disorder, and the revision separated it from agoraphobia at 6B02 so that the two can be diagnosed together rather than chosen between.

quiz.question: What makes a panic attack qualify as part of panic disorder rather than fear in a specific situation?
choices: That it is unexpected and not restricted to a particular stimulus or situation
That it lasts more than an hour
quiz.explanation: Panic disorder requires attacks that come out of the blue and are not bound to a particular situation, which is exactly the boundary ICD-11 draws against a specific phobia.

quiz.question: Why is anticipatory anxiety the feature that makes the disorder chronic?
choices: It is the most visible symptom
It maintains baseline arousal, which makes the next attack more likely and converts isolated events into a long-term condition
It only occurs in young people
quiz.explanation: Fear of the next attack keeps arousal elevated, which lowers the threshold for the following attack, so treating it is essential to converting the course.

quiz.question: What is a recognised harm of this presentation in primary care?
choices: Repeated unnecessary medical investigation driven by health anxiety
quiz.explanation: Presenting with physical complaints and requesting investigations is common, and iatrogenic harm from unnecessary testing is a documented consequence, which is one reason explaining the mechanism is part of treatment.

quiz.question: Which structure carries the interoceptive signal that is misread in a panic attack?
choices: The insula, which represents internal bodily state and relays it to the cingulate and amygdala
quiz.explanation: The insula represents internal bodily state and connects to the anterior cingulate and amygdala, so its amplification of a normal bodily change is the central step in the attack.

quiz.question: How does hyperventilation contribute to the attack?
choices: It lowers carbon dioxide, which amplifies the sensation of threat
It raises carbon dioxide and relieves the attack
quiz.explanation: Hyperventilation lowers carbon dioxide, which widens airways and increases the sense of breathlessness and of imminent catastrophe, so it is both a symptom and a maintaining mechanism.

quiz.question: What is the pharmacological principle for choosing a first drug?
choices: Prefer a drug the individual previously responded to, rather than switching class
Combine two SSRIs from the start
quiz.explanation: Guidelines advise reusing a previously effective drug rather than switching class, which is a specific and often overlooked point in panic disorder.

quiz.question: Why is a 5-HT1A partial agonist chosen when there is substance misuse?
choices: It gives anxiolysis without dependence, tolerance or withdrawal
It acts on the dopamine transporter
quiz.explanation: Buspirone's partial agonism at 5-HT1A produces anxiolysis with no dependence or withdrawal liability, which is its specific role in people with misuse problems.

quiz.question: What limits benzodiazepines in this disorder?
choices: Tolerance and dependence develop within weeks and they do not treat the avoidance that sustains the disorder
quiz.explanation: Benzodiazepines act quickly but produce tolerance and dependence within weeks and leave the learned avoidance untouched, so they are limited to short-term crisis use.

quiz.question: Why is full-dose treatment sometimes reached earlier than in depression?
choices: Because the target is avoidance and the avoidance has to be disinhibited before behavioural work can succeed
Because of the carbon dioxide level
quiz.explanation: Behavioural work cannot proceed while avoidance prevents engagement, so the drug target is behavioural access, which is why dose escalation may be needed sooner than in depression.

quiz.question: What is first-line psychotherapy and what does it change?
choices: Cognitive behavioural therapy, by testing the catastrophic interpretation and reversing avoidance
quiz.explanation: Cognitive behavioural therapy targets the misreading of bodily sensation and the safety behaviours that follow, which is why it can work where reassurance alone has not.

quiz.question: What is the practical definition of recovery in this disorder?
choices: Re-approaching avoided situations and restoring function, not merely fewer attacks
Being free of attack for one month
quiz.explanation: Because avoidance is what sustains the disorder, recovery is defined by going back to public transport, crowds and being alone, not by attack frequency alone.

quiz.question: How well do polygenic scores discriminate panic disorder in the largest study?
choices: Almost perfectly, making genetic diagnosis feasible
Modestly, with the best area under the curve around 0.60
quiz.explanation: Combining polygenic scores improved classification but the best area under the curve was about 0.60, which the authors describe as modest, so genetics has no diagnostic role.

quiz.question: Why does this page list the serotonin transporter gene for this disorder?
choices: Because it is a proven susceptibility gene
Because it encodes the pharmacological target of first-line treatment, and no susceptibility gene is established
Because it is the only gene studied
Because it explains the sex ratio
quiz.explanation: The gene listed encodes the target of first-line drug treatment rather than a risk gene, and this is stated explicitly so the distinction is not misread as a susceptibility finding.

quiz.question: Is there a validated diagnostic test for panic disorder?
choices: Yes, a carbon dioxide challenge in routine use
No; polygenic discrimination is weak and imaging findings are group-level model applications
quiz.explanation: Carbon dioxide challenge is an experimental research tool rather than a clinical test, and the genetics and imaging findings are group-level, so no test can diagnose an individual.

quiz.question: How do ICD-11 and previous classifications differ in how panic and agoraphobia are coded?
choices: They are now separate diagnoses that can be assigned together rather than alternatives
They were merged into one code
Panic was reclassified as a mood disorder
quiz.explanation: ICD-11 separated panic disorder from agoraphobia so that a person meeting both sets of requirements can receive both diagnoses, which is a substantive change from choosing one or the other.
